title: Query Evaluation: Processing Models
short: One tuple, one batch, or the whole result?
lead: The client may stop after one answer. Follow the requests, remembered positions, and work that still must finish before that first answer.
goals: Trace open, next, and close calls in the iterator model
Explain the state maintained by a selection, heap scan, and nested-loop join
Identify blocking operations such as sorting and hash-table construction
Explain pipelining, LIMIT, and iterator overhead

sections.title: Ask for the next answer, without building the whole result
sections.html:
Suppose a client wants the values greater than 5 from [2,7,4,9], multiplied by 10. We could first copy all four values, then build a second list [7,9], then a third list [70,90]. But the client may stop after its first answer. Why build everything before knowing whether it is needed?

Instead, give each processing step a small request: “return your next result.” A scan supplies stored values, a filter rejects values at most 5, and a projection calculates x×10. Put them together as Scan → Filter → Project. These arrows show data moving toward the client; requests move in the opposite direction.

This shared request interface is called the iterator model, also known as Volcano. Each operator implements open() to prepare its state, next() to return one tuple (row) or EOF, and close() to release resources. EOF means that no more rows exist, rather than a row containing NULL.

Client actionRequests and decisionsResult; next unread input
open()Project opens Filter; Filter opens ScanNo result yet; 2
first next()Scan gives 2: reject. Scan gives 7: keep. Project computes 7×1070; 4
second next()Scan gives 4: reject. Scan gives 9: keep. Project computes 9×1090; end
third next()Scan reports EOF; Filter and Project propagate itEOF; end
close()Close children and release scan resourcesFinished

Notice the first request: the filter reads two input rows to produce one output row. A parent knows only the interface; it need not know how many rows its child rejected. This is why the same projection can sit above a heap scan, a filter, or a join.

If the client stops after 70, which stored values remain unread?

4 and 9. The second root request never happens. Call close() anyway: stopping early does not release resources automatically.

Key takeaway

One parent next() call may invoke the child’s next() method several times. A filter must keep requesting input until it finds a qualifying tuple or reaches EOF.

sections.title: Remember where to resume; recognize where streaming stops
sections.html:
After returning 70, the plan must remember that the next stored value is 4. Restarting at 2 would return 70 forever. Each operator therefore keeps just the state needed to resume. The filter remembers its predicate and child; a heap scan remembers its current page and slot. The scan advances that position as it returns rows.

A join needs more state because one input row can match several rows on the other side. Try nested loops with outer keys [A,B] and inner keys [B,A,A]. The join keeps its current outer row and the next inner position.

RequestWork since the previous answerState after returning
1Hold outer A; compare inner B (no), then first A (yes)Return (A,A); next inner is second A
2Keep outer A; compare second A (yes)Return (A,A); inner is exhausted
3Restart inner; advance outer to B; compare first B (yes)Return (B,B); next inner is first A
4Finish both remaining A comparisons; no more outer rowsEOF

Neither a scan nor this filter has to wait for the complete input. Passing rows onward as soon as they are ready is pipelining. It avoids writing a whole intermediate result and reading it back.

Now insert an ascending sort before the projection. Seeing 7 does not establish the smallest qualifying value: an unread row could contain 6. A general sort of unordered input must examine every input row before its first sorted answer. This is a blocking boundary. In a two-pass external sort, open() can create sorted runs and next() can merge them; close() must delete temporary runs. A hash join similarly finishes building its hash table before probing it, although the probe phase can produce rows incrementally.

Thus LIMIT 1 saves later output work, but a LIMIT above this sort cannot skip reading the unordered input. Plan shape alone does not remove a blocking operation.

Key takeaway

LIMIT 1 above a sort may still require reading the entire input. To determine the first row in global order, the sort must consider rows that have not yet been read. A left-deep plan shape does not remove this blocking requirement.

Sources and teaching scope

Sources: PDF pages 7–13.

sections.title: Use batches when per-row calls become the work
sections.html:
The shared next() interface makes operators easy to combine, but a long analytical query may spend considerable CPU time making calls and restoring state. Suppose 100,000 rows pass through three operators without any reduction. One-row delivery makes about 100,000×3=300,000 row-delivery calls, excluding EOF. The useful arithmetic may be cheaper than that coordination.

Keep the same pull direction but return up to 1,000 rows per call. Each operator now delivers 100 batches, so the corresponding count is 100×3=300 batch calls. This vectorized model runs tight loops over a batch. SIMD means “single instruction, multiple data”: suitable hardware can apply an operation to several values at once. Batching makes that easier; it does not guarantee every operation uses SIMD.

A last batch need not be full. For 2,050 surviving rows, delivery is [1,000 rows], [1,000 rows], [50 rows], then EOF. Dropping the 50-row batch changes the query answer. A filter can also reduce a batch; an empty filtered batch does not necessarily mean the child's input has ended.

There is another option: let each operator finish its entire output before passing that output to its parent. This is the materialization model. Our example becomes [2,7,4,9] → [7,9] → [70,90]. Processing proceeds from completed child results upward, unlike the top-down requests of the iterator and vectorized models.

Keeping a complete small result can simplify processing and improve code and data locality: nearby instructions and values remain useful in cache. A very large intermediate can instead exhaust RAM or require temporary disk writes. The lecture associates batches with analytical workloads (OLAP) and small complete results with transaction workloads (OLTP). Treat these as workload tendencies, not a claim that one model always wins. A batch sort still needs to establish global order; changing delivery size does not remove its blocking dependency.

Would batch size 1,000 let LIMIT 1 avoid all unnecessary work?

No. The child may produce an entire batch before the parent takes one row. It can still save later batches. Compare first-answer latency, call overhead, and wasted work together.

sections.title: Exercise: trace the first two answers and cleanup
sections.html:
Use input [2,7,4,9,6] and the plan Scan → Filter(x>5) → Sort ascending → Project(x×10) → LIMIT 2. Before opening the answer, write down (1) every row the scan must read, (2) the filter output, (3) the sort output, and (4) the two client results. Decide whether LIMIT saves any input reads.

Follow the execution
  1. Opening/preparing the sort drains the filter. The scan reads all five values; the filter passes [7,9,6].
  2. The sort establishes [6,7,9]. For an external sort, this preparation can involve temporary runs. The exact number depends on memory.
  3. The first root next() obtains 6, projects 60, and returns it. The second obtains 7 and returns 70.
  4. LIMIT has enough rows. It stops asking, so 9 need not be projected to 90. close() must still propagate and remove temporary files.

The saved work is later delivery and projection, not reading the fifth input row: that row contained 6 and changed the smallest result. Without Sort, the same input order would yield 70 then 90 and could stop before reading 6, but that would answer a different ordering requirement.

Transfer the idea to a hash join: putting LIMIT above the join can save some probe work after answers arrive, but it does not automatically avoid building the hash table. Ask which preparation must finish before any valid answer can be returned.

Sources and teaching scope

Sources: PDF pages 9–13.

quiz.question: Can one Filter.next() call invoke child.next() more than once?
options: Yes, to discard tuples that do not satisfy the predicate
No, it always calls the child exactly once
Only when the child is an index
quiz.explanation: The filter continues reading input until it finds a qualifying tuple or reaches EOF.
